title: Positive Rosati trace pairing
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety] of dimension $g=\dim A$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], and put $E=\operatorname{End}_k(A)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, using module tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], where endomorphisms are group-scheme homomorphisms [def-sc-group-scheme] and multiplication is composition. Let $A^\vee=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{A/k}$ be the dual abelian variety of algebraically trivial invertible sheaves rigidified at the identity. Let $L$ be an ample [def-sc-ample] invertible sheaf [def-sc-invertible-module], and set $\lambda(x)=[t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1}]$ for translation $t_x$ by $x$. Then $\lambda$ has a two-sided inverse $\mu$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^\vee,A)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$. Pullback of invertible sheaves defines the dual $u^\vee$, extended $\mathbf Q$-linearly to rational homomorphisms, and $u^\dagger=\mu u^\vee\lambda$ defines a $\mathbf Q$-linear involution of $E$ reversing multiplication. There is a $\mathbf Q$-linear map $\operatorname{Tr}_A:E\to\mathbf Q$ whose image in $\mathbf Q_\ell$ equals $\operatorname{tr}(u\mid V_\ell A)$ for every prime $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$; here $V_\ell A$ is the rational Tate module [sk-def-av-tate] and $\operatorname{tr}$ is linear endomorphism trace [def-weil-endomorphism-trace]. It satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}_A(1)=2g$. The form $B_\lambda(u,v)=\operatorname{Tr}_A(u^\dagger v)$ is symmetric and $\mathbf Q$-bilinear, and $B_\lambda(u,u)>0$ for every nonzero $u\in E$.

source.place: Chapter I §14, printed p.61 (Rosati formula and involution), Theorem 14.3, printed p.62 (positive trace form); §11 p.53 (polarization isogeny); Proposition 10.20, printed pp.50–52 (trace on Tate modules).

proof.text: By [def-sc-ample], choose $r>0$ such that $L^r$ is very ample: there is a closed immersion $i:A\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$ with $i^*\mathcal O(1)\cong L^r$. Some coordinate $x_j$ does not vanish identically on $i(A)$, so $s=i^*x_j$ is a nonzero section of $L^r$. The variety $A$ is integral by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization], so its zero scheme $F=Z(s)$ is an effective Cartier divisor by [lem-pc-nonzero-section-integral-cartier]. That node also says that on an affine open $U$ where $L^r|_U=\mathcal O_Ue$ and $s|_U=ae$, the ideal $\mathcal I_F|_U$ is $a\mathcal O_U$ with $a$ a nonzerodivisor. Hence $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(s)$ maps $L^{-r}$ isomorphically onto $\mathcal I_F$ (locally $e^\vee\mapsto a$), and dualizing gives $\mathcal O_A(F)=\mathcal I_F^\vee\cong L^r$ [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle]. This sheaf is ample by [def-sc-ample] with exponent $1$, because $L^r$ is very ample. The criterion in [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus] makes $\phi_{L^r}$ an isogeny. The defining translation family gives $\phi_{L^r}=r\lambda$: on points $t_x^*L^r\otimes L^{-r}\cong(t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1})^{\otimes r}$. By [lem-sfb-simple-isogeny-decomposition], choose $h$ with $h(r\lambda)=[n]_A$ and $(r\lambda)h=[n]_{A^\vee}$, $n>0$. Then $\mu=(r/n)h$ has both required inverse identities in rational Hom. Empty $F$ is allowed in dimension zero.

source.place: §§8,11,14: polarization isogeny and rational inverse, pp.35–40,53,61

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-abelian-weil-pairing], dualization is additive, contravariant and preserves identities; extend it rationally and put $u^\dagger=\mu u^\vee\lambda$. Expanding gives $(u+v)^\dagger=u^\dagger+v^\dagger$, $(a u)^\dagger=a u^\dagger$ and $(uv)^\dagger=v^\dagger u^\dagger$, since $\lambda\mu=1$. For any $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$, write $e(x,y)=e_{A,\ell}(x,V_\ell(\lambda)y)$. Its nondegeneracy follows from perfection and the inverse $V_\ell(\mu)$; the pairing lemma gives alternation and $e(V_\ell(u)x,y)=e(x,V_\ell(u^\dagger)y)$. Skew symmetry then gives $e(x,V_\ell(u^{\dagger\dagger})y)=e(x,V_\ell(u)y)$. Nondegeneracy implies equality of these operators. Tate faithfulness in [lem-sfb-abelian-tate-action-saturation] implies equality in $E$: clear a rational denominator first, then apply its injectivity. Thus dagger is an involution.

If $g>0$, set $\operatorname{Tr}_A(u)=-[X^{2g-1}]P_u$ from [lem-sfb-abelian-tate-charpoly]. In a matrix determinant the coefficient of $X^{2g-1}$ is minus the sum of diagonal entries; hence this rational number has the required Tate traces for every $\ell$. Trace is the matrix diagonal sum of [def-weil-endomorphism-trace], so additivity and scalar linearity follow entry by entry and descend along the injective embedding $\mathbf Q\to\mathbf Q_\ell$. By [lem-sfb-abelian-tate-action-saturation], $\dim V_\ell A=2g$, so the identity has trace $2g$. If $g=0$, that same node gives a zero Tate module and injectivity of integral Hom, so $E=0$. Take the zero trace; all claims, including positivity for nonzero elements, are vacuous or zero identities in this case.

Trivialize the one-dimensional value line of $e$ and choose a basis of $V_\ell A$. If $J$ is its invertible pairing matrix and $U$ is the matrix of $u$, the adjoint identity is $U^{\mathsf t}J=JU^\dagger$. Therefore $U^\dagger=J^{-1}U^{\mathsf t}J$. The trace of this matrix is the trace of $U$: conjugation invariance is part of [def-weil-endomorphism-trace], and transpose preserves the diagonal sum. Descending to $\mathbf Q$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}_A(u^\dagger)=\operatorname{Tr}_A(u)$. Consequently
$\operatorname{Tr}_A(u^\dagger v)=\operatorname{Tr}_A((u^\dagger v)^\dagger)=\operatorname{Tr}_A(v^\dagger u)$.
This proves symmetry. Bilinearity follows by distributing multiplication and applying the two linear maps already constructed.

source.place: §14 pp.61–62, adjoint identity and bilinear form

proof.text:
For positivity assume $u\ne0$. Choose $n>0$ and an integral endomorphism $f$ with $nu=f\otimes1$. Injectivity of integral Hom in [lem-sfb-abelian-tate-action-saturation] implies it is torsion-free, so its map to rational Hom is injective and $f\ne0$. It suffices to prove positivity for $f$, since $B_\lambda(f,f)=n^2B_\lambda(u,u)$. The trace/intersection formula [lem-sfb-abelian-trace-intersection] gives
$$B_\lambda(f,f)=\frac{2g\,(L^{g-1}\cdot f^*L\cdot A)}{(L^g\cdot A)}.$$
Its hypotheses hold: $g>0$ by the zero case above, $L$ is ample, and $\mu$ has the two inverse identities of step 1. The denominator is positive by [lem-sc-positive-ample-hilbert-degree]; its Hilbert degree equals $(L^g\cdot A)$ by [def-sc-intersection-number], substituting $m=n_1+\cdots+n_g$ in the degree polynomial.

By [def-sc-ample], choose $r>0$ such that $L^r$ is very ample, with a closed immersion $i:A\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$ and $i^*\mathcal O(1)\cong L^r$. There is $x\in A(k)$ with $f(x)\ne0$: otherwise density from [lem-pc-rational-points-dense] and reducedness from [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization] force $f$ to be the zero morphism. Explicitly its equalizer with zero is closed since $A$ is separated; the equalizer ideal vanishes on the dense rational points and hence on the reduced source. A coordinate linear form for the immersion defined by $L^r$ can be chosen to vanish at $0$ and not at $f(x)$ (two distinct projective points give distinct one-dimensional quotients). Its pullback by $f$ is a section $s$ of $(f^*L)^r$, zero at $0$ and nonzero at $x$. Thus $Z(s)$ is nonempty and, by [lem-pc-nonzero-section-integral-cartier], is an effective Cartier divisor $H$. By [lem-sc-intersection-effective-cartier], $H$ is proper of dimension $g-1$, $L|_H$ is ample, and
$$((f^*L)^r\cdot L^{g-1}\cdot A)=(L^{g-1}\cdot H)>0,$$
the last inequality being [lem-sc-positive-ample-hilbert-degree] on $H$, including dimension zero.

source.place: Theorem 14.3 proof p.62: make the effective nonzero pullback explicit; Stacks varieties.tex Tags 0BEU,0BEV

proof.text: For completeness, intersection symmetry and scaling by a tensor power are elementary coefficient calculations in [def-sc-intersection-number]. Symmetry permutes the variables. For scaling in one slot use [lem-sc-snapper-numerical-polynomial]: the Euler polynomial has total degree at most $g$; substituting $n_1\mapsto rn_1$ multiplies its $n_1\cdots n_g$ coefficient by $r$. Hence the positive number in step 6 equals $r(f^*L\cdot L^{g-1}\cdot A)$. The numerator in step 5 is therefore positive. Since $2g>0$ and the denominator there is positive, $B_\lambda(f,f)>0$, and division by $n^2>0$ proves $B_\lambda(u,u)>0$.
